summary: Orange Control Room is a 2D pixel-art game that puts the player in the shoes of a space mission engineer, from the first plan to launch and mission control. The player chooses a mission with a budget, a deadline, and a target orbit, builds a rocket from 28 parts whose cost, mass, and performance come from published NASA figures, plans the burns on a real Keplerian orbit, then flies the mission from a control room where random events such as debris, solar flares, and engine failures demand emergency manoeuvres. A final score explains what each decision cost. Real missions are a chain of trade-offs: a better instrument is heavier, more mass needs more fuel, and more fuel costs money. Players rarely get to feel that whole chain. Orange Control Room lets them experience it in a short browser game.
details:
• What exactly does it do?
    • Orange Control Room puts the player in the shoes of a space mission engineer. The player designs a complete space mission, builds the rocket from real parts, plans the flight, and then runs it from a control room. At the end, the game scores the mission and explains what each decision cost.
    • The orange control room is a two-part game: planning and mission.
      • Planning: the player chooses a mission (budget, deadline, target orbit, required science and optional quests), then builds a rocket from 28 parts in four groups: engines, tank materials, telemetry and science instruments. Each part has a cost, mass, and performance taken or estimated from published NASA figures, and right-clicking a part shows its source. Cost, delta-v and weight update live, and warning lamps explain what stops a launch. The player then picks the launch angle and places engine burns on a real Keplerian orbit to raise, circularise, or adjust it.
      • Mission: the flight plays out in a control room at up to 1000x speed. The player sees only what the chosen telemetry parts can measure. Random events (satellite conjunction, debris shower, unknown asteroid, solar flare, engine malfunction, propellant leak, sensor failure) pause the flight and ask for an emergency manoeuvre. Orbit accuracy, budget, science delivered, and quests add up to a result from Failure to Scientific Breakthrough, and each score row explains why points were lost.
  • What benefits does it have?
    • The orange control room gives the player the experience of a mission control room: making decisions with limited information, limited money, and limited fuel, and living with the consequences. A real mission is a chain of trade-offs: a better instrument is heavier, a heavier payload needs more fuel, more fuel costs money, and the orbit you reach decides the science you get. Most learning tools teach one of these at a time; Orange Control Room puts the whole chain in one short game. It runs in a web browser with nothing to install, so it can be used in a classroom.
  • What do you hope to achieve?
    • We want people to learn how a space mission comes together: every engineering choice limits the next, and a failed mission teaches as much as a good one. Because missions, parts, and events are stored as data, teachers and players can add new missions and parts without writing code.
  • What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
    • Godot Engine 4.7.2 and GDScript
    • GitHub and GitHub Actions, which build the web version and publish it on GitHub Pages
    • Pixel art drawn by hand by our team, Orange Orbit
    • AI coding agents (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex), which wrote most of the code under the team's direction; every session is recorded in docs/AI_USAGE.md in the repository
    • NASA data for the parts, the planet, and the orbit mathematics (listed under NASA Data)
